content: Functional constipation in children is defined as chronic constipation without an identifiable underlying cause. It is a significant health issue, accounting for up to 25% of visits to pediatric gastroenterologists. Probiotics have been hypothesized to alter the gut microbiome in a way that promotes normal gut function and alleviates functional constipation. Several studies have explored this hypothesis, as well as the role of probiotics in other functional gastrointestinal disorders. A focused review of the evidence is necessary to evaluate the efficacy and safety of probiotics in managing chronic constipation in children. A systematic review was conducted to assess the efficacy and safety of probiotics for treating chronic constipation in children without a physical explanation. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included if they compared probiotics (or synbiotics) to placebo, no treatment, or other interventions in children aged 0 to 18 years diagnosed with functional constipation based on consensus criteria such as Rome IV. The search was conducted on June 28, 2021, across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and others, without restrictions on language, date, or publication type. Fourteen studies involving 1127 participants were included. Twelve studies evaluated probiotics for functional constipation, while two studies investigated synbiotics. Three studies compared probiotics to placebo regarding defecation frequency at the end of the study, but the results were not pooled due to significant heterogeneity. Four studies compared probiotics to placebo for treatment success, finding no clear difference in global improvement or treatment success (RR 1.29, 95% CI 0.73 to 2.26; low-certainty evidence). Five studies assessed withdrawals due to adverse events, with pooled results suggesting no difference between probiotics and placebo (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.21 to 1.95; low-certainty evidence). Three studies compared probiotics combined with an osmotic laxative to an osmotic laxative alone, finding no difference in defecation frequency (MD -0.01, 95% CI -0.57 to 0.56; low-certainty evidence). Two studies assessed global improvement or treatment success with this combination, again finding no difference (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.15; low-certainty evidence). Three studies evaluated withdrawals due to adverse events in this context, but the evidence was very uncertain (RR 2.86, 95% CI 0.12 to 68.35; very low-certainty evidence). Two studies compared probiotics to magnesium oxide, with very low-certainty evidence suggesting no clear difference in defecation frequency (MD 0.28, 95% CI -0.58 to 1.14), treatment success (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.57), or withdrawals due to adverse events (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.05 to 5.04). One study evaluated a synbiotic preparation compared to placebo, finding that synbiotics may lead to higher treatment success (RR 2.32, 95% CI 1.54 to 3.47; low-certainty evidence). No withdrawals due to adverse effects were reported in either group. Another study compared a synbiotic plus paraffin to paraffin alone, with very low-certainty evidence suggesting no difference in defecation frequency (MD 0.74, 95% CI -0.96 to 2.44) or treatment success (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.17). No adverse event-related withdrawals were reported. A third study compared a synbiotic to paraffin, with very low-certainty evidence suggesting no difference in defecation frequency (MD -1.53, 95% CI -3.00 to -0.06) or treatment success (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.13). Again, no withdrawals due to adverse effects were reported. Secondary outcomes were either not reported or reported in a manner that precluded analysis. Overall, there is insufficient evidence to determine whether probiotics are effective in treating chronic constipation in children or in altering defecation frequency. There is limited evidence from one study suggesting that synbiotics may be more effective than placebo in achieving treatment success, with no difference in adverse event-related withdrawals. There is insufficient evidence to draw conclusions about the efficacy or safety of probiotics when used in combination with or compared to other interventions. Most studies reported no serious adverse events, although two studies did not report on this outcome. Future research is needed to confirm the efficacy of probiotics, with guidance on their appropriate role in treatment hierarchies and alignment with core outcome sets to facilitate interpretation of findings.
